_about: Short alt text for Medium (read by kit/alt.mjs): figure id -> alt, at most 480 characters (the kit build fails over 500). Written only from each figure's own content (its .cap-area text and aria-labels); the article page keeps its long aria-labels. Pictures not listed keep the page's alt.
team-1: Team diagram for Day 1: one chat becomes a team. The lead started 72 agents and they started 201 more helpers, all set up that evening. I chat with the lead. Around the lead: 9 fix owners (wave 1, one topic each), 12 toolsmiths (one per incident), 12 reviewers and 11 architecture experts; from 23:06 agents report to mgmt-lead and mgmt-ops. Shared: main plus worktrees, incidents and findings, the chrome-measure lock with a short lane, the iPhone lease for my finger tests.
team-2: Team diagram for Day 2: I leave the chat. The lead started 88 agents. My steps and answers move to a new console, and timing gives way to counts. New that day: the console (steps, threads, proposals), an mgmt-ops hub for reports, 13 design engineers plus 5 claim verifiers, and iphone-runner, the first phone agent (06:49). Also 25 toolsmiths and 22 reviewers. Shared: a frozen snapshot pinned at 07:57, boards and v2 cards, the shared chrome-measure lane, iPhone and Simulator.
team-3: Team diagram for Day 3: owners reach me with proposals. The lead started 35 agents, and I decided 6 proposals in the console. Fix owners and 5 design engineers (heat, GPU, countdown) send proposals with a Try-it panel to the console. New that day: wi-stack, the first wave integrator, and a status board that shows waits and holds. Also mgmt-ops (ops-6, then ops-7), 14 toolsmiths, 11 reviewers, and iphone-runner recording only through ioscap; the iPhone was unplugged at 12:03.
team-4: Team diagram for Day 4: questions go to their owners. The lead started 48 agents. A thread router (topic map 18:28) sends each of my threads to the agent that owns its topic, so the lead wakes only for decisions. 8 fix owners answer my threads; iphone-runner owns the countdown threads. Also 7 design and architecture agents (memory, thread routing), mgmt-ops (ops-9, then ops-10), 19 toolsmiths and 8 reviewers. New: memory rules every agent loads, iPhone tests at Serious heat.
fig-6: Two charts of how fast each page warmed the iPhone, in degrees Celsius per minute, two sessions each. First: blank floor page minus 0.085 and minus 0.105, apple.com plus 0.055 and minus 0.013, Fastwork original plus 0.620 and plus 0.400, with fixes so far plus 0.192 and plus 0.238. Second, extra heat over the blank page on 11 October: original plus 0.467 and 0.491, v6 plus 0.255 and 0.319, final build g0.0m plus 0.255 and 0.336; v3 on 3 October plus 0.277 and 0.343.
team-5: Team diagram for Day 5: deputies and a device steward. The lead started 59 agents, 116 threads opened; roles turn proactive at 21:25. A desk (to 18:12), then a device steward (from 18:38), handles alarms, the iPhone and the chrome-measure queue. Also 7 fix owners who pull their next step, 2 integrators (int-v8, wave-v7), 13 design and architecture agents, 26 toolsmiths (90 incidents opened) and mgmt-ops-10, landing docs from 21:59. iPhone tests default to Xcode Serious.
team-6: Team diagram for Day 6: a cheaper team after a usage limit. The lead started 63 agents. The usage limit and an account switch came at 12:33; the new wiring was in place by 13:02. New: mgmt-clerk-1 on sonnet (mgmt-ops-10 parked), 25 one-shot second readers per phone ticket, 8 fix owners who hold the iPhone themselves, and an article crew of 10 (clips, visuals, pages). Also a device steward, int-v8, 9 toolsmiths and the thread router. iphone-runner was parked at 13:02.
team-7: Team diagram for Day 7: management winds down and owners take the phone. The lead started 31 agents and talks to owners directly; from 10:02 any agent may use a free iPhone. New: arch-compositor-morph, owner of the GPU end of the page, and int-v11 (wave integrator); the GPU playbook joins memory (16:10). Also 4 fix owners (hydrate, panel, People GPU), 4 reviewers, 7 mappers on sonnet, 4 toolsmiths and the thread router. Clerk and readers stop (last commits 09:50, 13:07).
team-8: Team diagram for Day 8: one small owner per flaw. The lead started 18 agents. A from-zero review began at 11:08 (arch-end-fresh, gpu-original), and the g0 line followed after 15:38: 6 g0 owners, one per visible flaw, each sending a proposal to the console; I rejected 2. The lead keeps a best-builds list, newest first. Also the integrator and GPU owner (int-v11, compositor-morph), 3 mappers on sonnet, 7 toolsmiths (USB link, test flakes) and a USB-link watchdog for the iPhone.
team-9: Team diagram for Day 9: same wiring, smaller owners. The lead started 17 agents. I probe WebKit borders and heat myself, and the lead repairs the phone link first. 4 g0 polish owners (box, menu, scroll, return) send proposals to the console; the lead adds 3 heat and off-screen agents. Also 6 mappers on sonnet, 5 toolsmiths (USB link, flakes) and the thread router. The best-builds list now also lists proposals by build, and the heat probe is kept in memory.
team-10: Team diagram for Day 10: from fixing to filming. The lead started 18 agents over the full UTC day (the day line counts 11 up to 12:57). I call it done at 10:56. The lead spawns a film crew: cap-worst films the worst moments for an article crew of 10 writers and day summarisers. Also 2 fix owners (deck chrome, reveal paint), 3 mappers on sonnet, 2 toolsmiths and the thread router. g0.0l is the best build that day, and pictures from iPhone recordings are allowed.
team-11: Team diagram for Day 11, the epilogue: my own thumb, then a film crew. The lead started 20 agents. fix-reveal-paint lands g0.0m at 03:38. My own swipes (C-146) become console steps, and 3 capture agents replay my swipe on the iPhone with a robot. An article crew of 11 makes clips, histograms and GIFs; 3 researchers look at video hosting (on sonnet); 3 agents review, audit and edit the article. The thread router still sends threads to the topic owner.
fig-9: Fig. 9: slow frames (over 34 ms) and very slow frames (over 50 ms) in my swipe through the top of the page, in four moments, original against the final build g0.0m, from the phone's own frame log. All four moments, my own finger: 88 slow (33 very slow) on the original, 4 (0) on g0.0m. The robot replaying one of my swipes (the 11.5 s of clip 1, Serious heat): 104 (47) on the original, 9 (2) on g0.0m. My finger records were 15.1 s and 18.9 s, not the same strokes.
fig-10: Fig. 10: in ten days the team landed 29 fixes in a best build without asking me (8 from wave 1, 14 later fixes no proposal touched, 7 follow-ups inside topics I had accepted, 1 more on Day 11). It dropped 29 experiments on its own measurements before they reached me (the lead 21, the fix owners at least 8). 41 proposals came to me: I accepted 36; 4 were rejected, withdrawn or sent back; 1 stayed a draft.
team-0: Diagram of who talks to whom: the whole team by Day 11, in the same positions as the day diagrams, tags give each part's first and last day in use. I talk to the lead and the console, which feeds the lead and a thread router to the fix owners. The lead runs fix owners, toolsmiths, architecture and design, phone and capture agents, and the article crew. Dashed, not used on Day 10 or 11: the management hub, desk and steward, architecture and design, integrators.
lessons-numbers: Four cards on what we could have saved. 1, aim at the GPU from day 1: 1.5 to 2 of the 8.7 days. 2, measure my swipe first: 0.5 to 1.5 days; slow frames under my finger matched my pick 7 of 7 times, Chrome and robot numbers 3 of 8. 3, a second quiet Mac: 70 to 200 of the 140 to 220 hours agents waited for the Mac. 4, keep the cache: about $2,760 of the $10,930 bill went to re-reading. All four together: about 6 to 7 days instead of 8.7, and $3,000 to 5,500 less.
